transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi. Yeah, thank you for seeing me. So, um, I guess the main reason I finally decided to come in is because I am just tired all the time. And I mean, I know I’m a teacher, and people always say, 'Oh, you work with kids all day, of course you're exhausted.' But it’s really not that normal teacher-at-the-end-of-the-day tired, if that makes sense? It's different. It feels like... well, even after I get a completely full night’s sleep, I wake up and I'm already dreading the day because I just have absolutely no energy. 

And by the time I get home, the evening is just a struggle. I literally have to force and push myself through every single little thing. Just sitting down to do my grading feels like climbing a mountain, and then there's trying to figure out dinner, and just going through the motions of getting my things ready for the next morning... it takes everything out of me. I used to be able to just bounce back, but now I'm dragging myself through the week, and I just can't seem to shake this exhaustion no matter how much I rest.
Have you noticed that you don’t enjoy things as much as you used to, or that you’ve lost interest in activities you once found pleasurable?

Um, no, not really. I wouldn't say I've lost interest in things. I mean, I still really love my hobbies and everything. Like, I still love reading. I'm actually in this book club with a few of the other teachers from my school, and a couple of the girls from the middle school across town, and we meet once a month. And I still really, really look forward to that. I love getting into a good mystery novel—we just read this one thriller that was set in the 1920s, and I was completely hooked, just like I always am. 

So the enjoyment is definitely still there. It's just... well, sometimes I might not read as many chapters in one sitting as I used to, but that's purely because my eyes are getting heavy and I just can't keep them open, not because I don't care about the story. And it's the exact same thing with my gardening. I have these raised beds in my backyard, and I still get so excited when my tomatoes start coming in. I was just out there this past weekend checking on them. I might need to take more breaks while I'm weeding because, like I was saying before, my energy is just so incredibly low, but I still love being out there in the dirt. 

So, yeah, I still enjoy all the things I've always enjoyed. I still want to do them. It's really just the energy part that gets in the way, you know? But the actual feeling of liking them? That hasn't changed at all. I still want to go to the farmer's market on Sundays, I still want to see my friends... I just wish I wasn't so completely drained while I was trying to do those things.
Would you say that you’ve been feeling down, sad, or hopeless most days?

Well, um, down or sad? I guess... I mean, it's not like I'm crying all the time or anything like that. I'm not, you know, sobbing in the staff bathroom between periods. Most days I can still put on a smile for my students—I teach fourth grade, so you really have to be "on" for them, you know? You have to have that energy, or at least fake it, because they pick up on everything. So I get through the lessons, I do the spelling tests, I do the math worksheets, and I smile and I encourage them. 

But... underneath all of that, it just feels like there’s this constant, heavy, gray feeling. It's just so flat. And it follows me everywhere. It follows me home, into my car, into my house. Even when I was talking about my garden before, or when I pull out my watercolors—which I also love to do on weekends when the light is good in my dining room—it’s like those things feel sort of... far away? Like there's a pane of glass between me and the things I'm doing. It’s not that I don't want to do them, like I said, but this grayness just sits there. It’s been there for so long now, just this lingering flatness that I can't shake off, even when I'm technically having a good time. It’s hard to explain, but it’s just this persistent, low-level sadness that never really leaves me alone, no matter how hard I try to push past it for the kids or for myself.
Have you found yourself feeling like you’re not good enough, or blamed yourself for things more than usual, even when it wasn’t really your fault?

Well, yeah, I guess I do... I mean, I really struggle with feeling like I'm just not doing enough, or that I'm not good enough anymore. It's like this constant loop in my head. I keep thinking, you know, I should be handling everything better. I’m a professional, I’ve been teaching for years, I have my master's degree, I should be able to manage a fourth-grade classroom and my own life without feeling like I'm drowning. But then, like, the other day, I was sitting down to do my lesson plans for the upcoming week—just the standard math and language arts modules we always do—and it literally took me twice as long as it normally would. I just sat there staring at the curriculum guide, feeling completely incompetent. 

And it's not just the planning. Last week, my principal asked if I would consider mentoring one of the new student teachers who's coming in next semester. Normally, I would love that. I love helping new teachers get their footing. But I just... I had to say no. I told her I didn't think I had the bandwidth right now. And ever since I said no, I've just been beating myself up about it. I keep telling myself that I’m letting my school down, that I'm letting my principal down, and honestly, that I'm letting my family down, too, because I come home and I'm just so useless. I just feel like I should be stronger, or more capable, and when I can't keep up with the things I used to do so easily, I just feel like a complete failure. It's really hard to shake that feeling that I'm just not measuring up to what everyone expects of me, or what I expect of myself.
Have you noticed any changes in your ability to think clearly, concentrate, or make decisions lately?

Um, no, not really. I wouldn't say my thinking is clouded or anything like that. My concentration is actually still pretty sharp, thankfully. I mean, like I was saying about my lesson plans taking longer earlier—that was really more about just feeling overwhelmed and incompetent, not that I couldn't focus on the words on the page, you know? 

Because, for example, just yesterday afternoon, I had to grade thirty-two math assessments. We're doing long division right now, which is always just a complete nightmare to grade because you really have to look at every single step of their work. If you just look at the final answer, you have no idea if they messed up the actual division part or if they just made a silly subtraction error in the middle. So you have to be really, really dialed in. And I sat there at my kitchen table, with my red pen and a cup of chamomile tea, and I got through the entire stack without losing my place or getting distracted at all. I was completely focused on it. 

And as for making decisions... well, honestly, teaching fourth grade is basically just making a hundred rapid-fire decisions every single minute. You're constantly assessing the room—like, do I let Tommy go to the bathroom right now or make him wait until after the spelling quiz? Do I step in and stop that little argument over the blue dry-erase marker, or do I let them practice their conflict resolution skills? And I'm still doing all of that just fine. I haven't had any trouble deciding what to do in the classroom, or even at home, like deciding what to make for dinner or picking out which watercolor paints to use. My brain still works exactly the way it always has, and my thoughts are perfectly clear. It's really just the physical exhaustion and that... that heavy grayness I mentioned before. But the actual thinking and concentrating part? No, I haven't noticed any issues with that at all.
Have you noticed that you're moving more slowly than usual, or that even small tasks take you longer to start or finish, even if your mind still feels clear?

Well, moving more slowly? I don't think so. I mean, I really haven't noticed anything like that. I'm definitely not walking around like I'm moving through molasses or anything. Like I said, I teach fourth grade, and you just can't move slowly when you have twenty-eight nine-year-olds in a room. You're constantly on your feet. You're walking up and down the aisles, checking their work, leaning over desks to point out where they forgot to carry the one, rushing to the front of the room to write on the whiteboard, then rushing to the back to grab more construction paper... it's just non-stop motion. 

And even when I'm at home, I don't feel like I'm moving sluggishly. I still get up, make my coffee, feed the cat—he's a Maine Coon mix, so he gets very vocal if his breakfast is late, which means I can't exactly dawdle in the mornings. I still do my normal routine at my normal pace. I mean, sure, I'm exhausted, like I told you, and I feel that heavy grayness, but my actual physical movements? No, they're the same as always. 

And as for tasks taking longer to start or finish... well, no, not really. I mean, yes, the lesson planning took longer that one day, but like I explained, that was because I was sitting there feeling so overwhelmed and incompetent, not because I was physically slow to start writing or typing. Once I actually get going on a task, I just do it. Like grading those math tests, or when I decide to do a load of laundry on Saturday morning. I don't sit there for an hour staring at the washing machine trying to force myself to put the clothes in. I just sort the darks from the lights, pour the detergent, and start the cycle. It's just the normal pace of life, really. So, no, I haven't noticed any physical slowness or delays in getting things done. It's just that the things I'm doing feel so heavy while I'm doing them, if that makes sense.
Have you ever had periods in the past where you felt this way before, or is this the first time you've experienced something like this?

Um, well, it's not really that I've had periods of this in the past where it comes and goes, like a rollercoaster or anything. It’s more like... it’s just been this one long, continuous stretch. If I really sit down and trace it back, look at the calendar, I’d say this has been going on for about two years and two months now. Yes, exactly two years and two months. 

I know the timeline so well because I remember exactly when it started. It was right around the time my husband stopped working outside the home. He transitioned to being at home, and our entire household routine just... completely flipped upside down. Before that, we had this very set, predictable schedule, you know? We would both get up at 6:00 AM, we’d navigate the kitchen together, make our coffee—it was like this little choreographed dance we had down to an absolute science—and then we’d both commute out to our respective jobs. 

But then his situation changed, and suddenly he was home all day. Which is fine, of course, I mean, it made sense for us at the time, but it just completely altered the dynamic of the house in ways I wasn't prepared for. I was still getting up at the crack of dawn to go wrangle twenty-eight fourth graders, and he was suddenly on this totally different rhythm. He was sleeping in a bit later, or doing things around the house during the day, and it just threw everything off balance. The division of chores shifted, the way we spent our evenings shifted, even just the feeling of walking through the front door after a long, exhausting day of teaching changed, because he'd already been in that space all day long. 

And that's really when this heavy, gray feeling I mentioned earlier started creeping in. I honestly thought it was just an adjustment period at first, you know? Just a bump in the road while we figured out our new normal and how to exist in the same house with two completely different daily structures. I kept telling myself I just needed to get used to the new routine. But then a month went by, and then six months, and then a year, and it just never lifted. So, no, it hasn't been separate episodes. It's just been this one, solid block of feeling this way for over two years, ever since our lives shifted like that.

Have you ever had a period of time where you felt unusually high-spirited, extremely energetic, or so irritable that you were snapping at people more than usual—maybe even doing things that were out of character for you, like spending a lot of money, taking on too many projects, or not sleeping much but still feeling rested?

Oh, goodness, no. No, definitely not. I can't even imagine having that kind of energy, to be honest. 

I mean, not sleeping much but still feeling rested? Oh, I wish! If I don't get my full seven to eight hours, I am just completely useless the next day. I really need my sleep. My husband knows, the cat knows—if I'm not in bed by 10:00 PM, the next morning is going to be incredibly rough. I've never had a time in my life where I could just skip sleep and feel fine. My body just absolutely does not work that way. 

And as for spending a lot of money... well, on a teacher's salary, that's not really an option anyway! I mean, sure, I buy the occasional extra set of dry-erase markers or some nice seasonal borders for my bulletin boards out of pocket—because, let me tell you, the school budget never actually covers what you need to make a classroom functional and welcoming—but I am very, very careful with our finances. I've always been the one who balances the accounts and tracks our monthly expenses, which has been especially important since my husband transitioned to being at home. I would never just go out and blow a bunch of money on a whim. That would stress me out so much, I wouldn't even be able to enjoy whatever it was I bought. 

And taking on too many projects... no, I stick to my lesson plans, my grading, and keeping the house running. I don't get these sudden urges to, I don't know, remodel the kitchen or start an after-school drama club or anything like that. I know my limits. 

And I really don't snap at people either. You have to have an incredible amount of patience to do what I do for a living. If little Jimmy asks me how to spell "because" for the fifth time in a single hour, I can't just snap at him. I just take a deep breath, smile, and help him sound it out again. I'm very even-keeled when it comes to my temper. So, no, I've never had a period where I was acting out of character or bouncing off the walls or feeling unusually high-spirited. It’s really just been this steady, heavy, gray feeling I’ve been dealing with for the last two years. Nothing on the complete opposite end of the spectrum like you're describing.

Looking back over this time, would you say there have been periods lasting at least two weeks where you didn't enjoy or get pleasure from most things you usually enjoy, even things like reading or gardening?

Oh, no, not at all. I haven't lost my interest in things like that. I actually still read quite a bit. I mean, I have to read a lot for school, obviously, previewing chapter books for the kids—right now we're doing *Because of Winn-Dixie*, which is just such a classic, and I still get a little teary at the end every single time, even after teaching it for six years. But I still read for my own pleasure, too. I'm in a little book club with a few of the other teachers from my district, and I always make sure to finish the book. I still really look forward to our meetings, even if I'm tired. 

And it's funny you mention gardening, because while I don't have a huge outdoor garden—our yard isn't really set up for that—I do have quite a collection of indoor plants. I have some pothos, a couple of monsteras, and this one very, very finicky fiddle leaf fig that I've somehow managed to keep alive for three years now, which I'm honestly quite proud of. I still really enjoy taking care of them. Every Sunday morning, that's my routine. I get my little copper watering can, I check the soil, I wipe down the leaves... it's very grounding for me. Even with my husband being home all day now and the house feeling a bit more crowded, tending to my plants is my quiet time. And the cat usually follows me around while I do it, trying to bat at the lower leaves of the spider plant. 

So, no, I haven't had any periods where I just stopped enjoying those things or didn't want to do them. I still look forward to them. I still get pleasure from them. It's just that, like I said before, there's that heavy, gray feeling kind of sitting in the background of my life, but the actual enjoyment of my hobbies hasn't gone away. I still like my books and my plants and my quiet Sunday mornings just as much as I always did. I've never had a stretch of time, definitely not two whole weeks, where I just didn't care about them anymore. I think I'd be absolutely devastated if I lost my love for reading, honestly, because it's such a big part of who I am and how I decompress after dealing with twenty-eight kids all week.
Have you been feeling that you are a failure or that you have let people down more days than not?

I mean, I wouldn't necessarily use the word "failure," because that sounds so... final, I guess? But I definitely have this constant, nagging feeling that I'm just not measuring up. I keep thinking I should be handling everything so much better than I am. We’re adults, right? We’re supposed to be able to adapt to changes. 

But... well, for example, my lesson plans. I’ve been teaching fourth grade for six years now, so I have the curriculum down pat. I know exactly how to teach equivalent fractions, I know how to guide them through their first real state history project. But lately, when I sit down to do my planning for the week, it just takes me twice as long. I’ll sit at the kitchen island with my laptop and my planner, and I just... I can't seem to get through it efficiently anymore. I just stare at the screen. And then I feel terrible because that’s time I could be spending with my husband, or time I could be using to actually contribute to the household. I feel like I'm letting him down, letting my family down, because I'm always just bogged down in work that absolutely shouldn't be taking me that long. 

And it bleeds into my actual job, too, which is what really gets to me. Just a few weeks ago, my principal asked me if I would consider mentoring a newer teacher who just joined the district. She’s fresh out of college, very sweet, but completely overwhelmed by the paperwork. And usually, I love that kind of thing. I love sharing my organizational templates and my classroom management strategies—I use this whole token economy system that the kids just adore, and it works wonders for behavior. But I just... I had to say no. I couldn't do it. I told her I just didn't have the bandwidth this year to take on a mentee. 

And ever since I said that, it’s just been eating away at me. I tell myself I’m letting my school down, letting this poor new teacher down, just because I can't seem to get my own act together. It’s like this loop in my head. I’m a veteran teacher now, I should be a leader in my grade-level team, but instead, I'm just barely keeping my own head above water. So, yes, I do feel like I'm letting people down, pretty much constantly, because I just can't seem to push past this heavy feeling and be the capable person everyone needs me to be.
Have you ever had even a few days in a row where you felt unusually upbeat, energetic, or like you didn’t need as much sleep, even if it didn’t last long?

No, really, not even for a few days. I know you asked about a longer stretch a minute ago, but honestly, even a two- or three-day weekend of feeling like that is completely foreign to me. I just don't have those kinds of spikes in my mood or my energy. 

I mean, if I have a good day—which does happen, you know, I’m not crying in the supply closet or anything—a good day for me just means I got through my teaching and my grading without feeling like I was wading through molasses, or maybe I actually had the energy to cook a proper dinner instead of just asking my husband to heat up some leftovers. But it’s never this unusually upbeat, super-energized state where I feel like I can take on the world. 

Like, just to give you an example, last month we had parent-teacher conferences. And the way our district schedules them, it is just brutal. We teach a full day on Thursday, the kids dismiss at 3:15, and then conferences run from 4:00 PM all the way until 8:00 PM. You have these parents coming in back-to-back, every fifteen minutes, and you have to be completely "on," you know? You have to be positive and constructive, even when you're trying to gently explain to a parent why their child is still struggling with basic multiplication tables. And by the time I get home at 8:45, I am completely and utterly depleted. I don't get a second wind. I don't suddenly feel wired or like I can skip sleep. I just want to put on my pajamas, wash my face, and collapse into bed. 

So, no, I’ve never had even a short little burst where I felt like I didn't need rest or where I was unusually high-spirited. Even on my absolute best days, I still very much need my sleep, and my energy is just... normal, I guess? Or, well, lately, just lower than normal because of this constant heavy feeling. But never higher. I've never experienced anything like what you're describing, not even for a day or two.
Have you had a depressed mood most of the day, more days than not, for at least two years?

Well, yes, I suppose so. Two years... yes, it’s definitely been that long, if not longer. It's not like I'm sobbing every day, you know? I think people hear "depressed" and they picture someone who can't get out of bed, but that's just not me. I have a job to do. I have twenty-eight fourth graders depending on me, and you can't just check out when you're in a classroom. You have to be present. You have to put on a face. 

So most days, I can still smile for my students. I can get through the lessons—like I said, we're reading *Because of Winn-Dixie*, and I can still put all the right inflection into my voice when I read aloud, and I can still get excited when a student finally grasps how to do long division. I can still go through all the motions. But underneath all of that... it just feels like there’s this gray, flat feeling. It’s just always there, kind of humming in the background. 

And the hardest part is that it doesn't stay at school. It follows me home. I'll walk through the door, and my husband will ask how my day was, and I just feel... heavy. It’s like all the energy I spent smiling for the kids just drains out of me the second I put my keys on the counter. And then, even the things I normally love, like tending to my plants or getting out my watercolors—which I haven't done much of lately, to be honest—they just seem so far away. It’s like I’m looking at my own life through a foggy window. 

I’ll sit on the couch, and I know I should get up and check on my fiddle leaf fig, or maybe sketch something, but that gray feeling just settles over me. It’s not a sharp, stabbing kind of sadness. It’s just... flat. And it’s been like this for a really long time. I honestly can't remember the last time I went a whole week without feeling that heaviness pulling at me, so yes, it's definitely been more days than not for at least two years. It just feels like this is my baseline now, this constant, quiet grayness.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight over the last couple of years, like eating more or less than usual or gaining or losing weight without trying?

No, not really. My weight has been pretty much exactly the same since... well, since before we got married, honestly. You'd think with how stressful teaching can be, or with this constant heavy feeling I’ve been having, that I might stress-eat, or maybe skip meals because I'm too drained, but I'm actually very regimented about my food. I kind of have to be, with the school bell schedule. 

Our lunch period is exactly at 11:35 every single day, and we only get thirty minutes, which includes walking the kids to the cafeteria. So I always pack my lunch the night before, usually the same kind of things—a turkey and spinach wrap, maybe some baby carrots with hummus, and an apple. I eat in the teachers' lounge with Mrs. Davis, the fifth-grade teacher next door, and I always finish my whole lunch. It's just like clockwork. My appetite there hasn't changed a bit.

And then for dinner, even when I'm feeling that grayness I was telling you about, and I just want to collapse on the couch and I don't really have the energy to cook, I still eat a normal amount. My husband is really wonderful about that. If I'm too exhausted to make the chicken stir-fry or whatever we had written on our meal-prep whiteboard for the week, he'll step in and make some pasta, or we'll just order from that little Thai place down the street. I still enjoy the food, and I eat a regular portion. 

I know some people completely lose their appetite when they feel down, or on the flip side, they sit and eat a whole sleeve of cookies, but I just... I eat my regular three meals. It's probably the only thing in my day-to-day routine right now that feels completely unaffected by everything else. I still fit into all the exact same work trousers I bought three years ago for back-to-school. So, no, my weight hasn't fluctuated at all, either up or down, and my appetite is just exactly what it's always been.
Have you felt worthless or guilty, like you don’t deserve to be happy or that you’re a burden to others, more days than not?

Well... I don't know if I'd use the exact word 'worthless,' that sounds a bit extreme, but guilty? Yes. Oh, absolutely, yes. It’s just... I constantly have this running dialogue in my head that I should be handling everything better than I am. Because on paper, my life is fine, you know? I have a good job, a supportive husband. But I just can't seem to keep up the way I used to, and that really eats away at me. 

Like, just to give you an idea, my lesson plans. I used to be able to sit down on a Sunday afternoon, maybe put on some light music, and knock out my entire week's plans in an hour or two. Now? It takes me twice as long, at least. I'll just sit there staring at the state standards, trying to figure out the reading blocks, and it just drags on and on. And because it takes so long, it completely eats up my weekend, which means I'm not spending any real quality time with my husband. So then I start telling myself I'm a terrible wife, that I'm letting my family down because I'm just sitting at the kitchen table stressing over fourth-grade spelling lists instead of being present with him. 

And it bleeds into my professional life, too. Just last month, our principal asked if I would be the official mentor for one of the new hires—this sweet girl who just took over a third-grade classroom and is clearly in over her head. A couple of years ago, I would have jumped at the chance. I used to love helping new teachers set up their bulletin boards and figure out their classroom management. But I just... I had to say no. I knew I didn't have it in me. And honestly, ever since I said no, every time I see her looking frazzled by the copy machine, I just feel this crushing guilt. I tell myself I’m letting my school down, I'm letting my colleagues down. It's just this heavy, nagging feeling that no matter what I do, I'm just falling short and being a disappointment to the people who rely on me.
Have there been times when even the things you usually enjoy, like reading or gardening, felt completely uninteresting or empty, even if just for a few days in a row?

Well, no, not really. I wouldn't say they feel uninteresting or empty. It's more... well, like I was saying before about my watercolors and my plants, the interest is definitely still there. I still love them. I really do. 

Like, my fiddle leaf fig—I was actually just looking at it yesterday morning before I left for school, because I noticed the top leaves were getting a little dusty, and I still get that little spark of satisfaction when I wipe them down with a damp cloth and they get all shiny and green again. I still care about it very much. And I have a whole collection of succulents on the windowsill above the kitchen sink, and I still check the soil, I still rotate them so they get even sunlight. I still *want* to do these things. 

And with the watercolors... I know I said I haven't been doing it as much lately, but it's absolutely not because I don't care or because it feels empty. If I actually make myself sit down and get my paints out, and I get my good brushes—I have these really nice sable brushes my husband got me for our anniversary a few years ago, they hold water beautifully—I still really enjoy mixing the colors. I still love seeing how the pigment spreads on the wet paper, you know, doing those wet-on-wet washes. It's just that sometimes that heavy, flat feeling I mentioned makes it hard to find the physical energy to set up the water cup and tape down the paper. But the actual interest? The enjoyment? That's definitely still there once I'm doing it. 

And reading! Oh, I still read all the time. I'm actually in a book club with some of the other teachers. We meet once a month, usually at Mrs. Davis's house—she's the fifth-grade teacher I eat lunch with—though sometimes we'll go to this little bakery downtown if nobody wants to host. But I always finish the book. Even if I'm completely exhausted from grading papers, I'll curl up in bed with my Kindle, and I still get completely pulled into the story. I still laugh at the funny parts, I still get invested in what happens to the characters. 

So, no, I don't think I've ever had a time, not even for a few days, where my hobbies felt completely uninteresting. The enjoyment hasn't gone away at all. It's just... sometimes it feels like I have to wade through that gray tiredness to get to it, if that makes sense? But the things I love are still the things I love.
Have you had trouble staying asleep or found yourself waking up much earlier than usual, even when you didn't have to get up for work or anything?

Well, no, not at all. Once my head hits the pillow, I am completely out for the night. I don't have any trouble staying asleep, and I certainly don't wake up early on my own. 

I actually have a very strict bedtime routine, which I think helps. I usually start winding down around 9:30 PM because teaching fourth graders all day just completely wires your brain, and you have to consciously transition out of that mode. So I'll wash my face, put on this lavender lotion my sister got me for Christmas—it’s supposed to be really calming, and I actually do think the scent helps signal to my brain that the day is over—and then I'll read on my Kindle for about twenty minutes or so. By 10:15, my husband turns off his bedside lamp, and I am usually fast asleep by 10:30. 

And I don't wake up in the middle of the night, ever. My husband sometimes gets up to get a glass of water or to check the thermostat, because our upstairs gets weirdly drafty in the winter and he runs hot, but I sleep right through all of it. I'm a very heavy sleeper. 

As for waking up early... definitely not. My alarm goes off at 5:45 AM every single weekday. I use one of those sunrise alarm clocks, you know the ones? They gradually get brighter starting thirty minutes before the actual sound goes off, to mimic a natural sunrise. It’s supposed to be a lot less jarring than a traditional beeping alarm, which I need because I am not naturally a morning person. But honestly, even with that light getting brighter and brighter right next to my face, I never, ever wake up before the actual birdsong noise starts playing at 5:45. 

And on weekends? Oh, if I didn't have anything planned, I could easily sleep until 8:30 or 9:00. I never find myself just popping awake at dawn for no reason. If anything, because of that heavy, drained feeling I've been talking about, I usually want to stay in bed *longer*. The bed just feels so warm and safe, and it's so hard to push the covers off and face the day. So I definitely don't have that problem where people wake up at 3 AM and just stare at the ceiling with their mind racing. I sleep completely through the night, every night, just like a log.

Looking back over the last two years, have there ever been two weeks or more when you stopped getting pleasure from things you usually enjoy, like reading or tending to your plants, even if you still did them?

Two weeks? No... no, honestly, not even for two weeks. I know we were just talking about my hobbies, but even if I really think back over the whole last two years, there was never a block of time like that where I just stopped getting pleasure from them. 

Like, if I think about... well, let's take the winter before last. We had that massive snowstorm right around winter break, do you remember that? They actually had to delay the start of the spring semester by two days because the plows couldn't clear the neighborhood streets fast enough, and we were completely snowed in. target_item.manifestation: I keep thinking I should be handling everything better, and when my lesson plans take twice as long or I say no to mentoring a newer teacher, I tell myself I’m letting my family and my school down.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question directly asks about feeling like a failure or letting people down, which matches the description and manifestation of low self-esteem.

patient.answer:
I mean, I wouldn't necessarily use the word "failure," because that sounds so... final, I guess? But I definitely have this constant, nagging feeling that I'm just not measuring up. I keep thinking I should be handling everything so much better than I am. We’re adults, right? We’re supposed to be able to adapt to changes. 

But... well, for example, my lesson plans. I’ve been teaching fourth grade for six years now, so I have the curriculum down pat. I know exactly how to teach equivalent fractions, I know how to guide them through their first real state history project. But lately, when I sit down to do my planning for the week, it just takes me twice as long. I’ll sit at the kitchen island with my laptop and my planner, and I just... I can't seem to get through it efficiently anymore. I just stare at the screen. And then I feel terrible because that’s time I could be spending with my husband, or time I could be using to actually contribute to the household. I feel like I'm letting him down, letting my family down, because I'm always just bogged down in work that absolutely shouldn't be taking me that long. 

And it bleeds into my actual job, too, which is what really gets to me. Just a few weeks ago, my principal asked me if I would consider mentoring a newer teacher who just joined the district. She’s fresh out of college, very sweet, but completely overwhelmed by the paperwork. And usually, I love that kind of thing. I love sharing my organizational templates and my classroom management strategies—I use this whole token economy system that the kids just adore, and it works wonders for behavior. But I just... I had to say no. I couldn't do it. I told her I just didn't have the bandwidth this year to take on a mentee. 

And ever since I said that, it’s just been eating away at me. I tell myself I’m letting my school down, letting this poor new teacher down, just because I can't seem to get my own act together. It’s like this loop in my head. I’m a veteran teacher now, I should be a leader in my grade-level team, but instead, I'm just barely keeping my own head above water. So, yes, I do feel like I'm letting people down, pretty much constantly, because I just can't seem to push past this heavy feeling and be the capable person everyone needs me to be.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has had any periods of elevated mood or increased energy that were noticeably different from their usual self, even if brief.
doctor.question: Have you ever had even a few days in a row where you felt unusually upbeat, energetic, or like you didn’t need as much sleep, even if it didn’t last long?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of hypomania (feeling unusually upbeat, energetic, or needing less sleep for a few days), which is not covered by any of the items in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, really, not even for a few days. I know you asked about a longer stretch a minute ago, but honestly, even a two- or three-day weekend of feeling like that is completely foreign to me. I just don't have those kinds of spikes in my mood or my energy. 

I mean, if I have a good day—which does happen, you know, I’m not crying in the supply closet or anything—a good day for me just means I got through my teaching and my grading without feeling like I was wading through molasses, or maybe I actually had the energy to cook a proper dinner instead of just asking my husband to heat up some leftovers. But it’s never this unusually upbeat, super-energized state where I feel like I can take on the world. 

Like, just to give you an example, last month we had parent-teacher conferences. And the way our district schedules them, it is just brutal. We teach a full day on Thursday, the kids dismiss at 3:15, and then conferences run from 4:00 PM all the way until 8:00 PM. You have these parents coming in back-to-back, every fifteen minutes, and you have to be completely "on," you know? You have to be positive and constructive, even when you're trying to gently explain to a parent why their child is still struggling with basic multiplication tables. And by the time I get home at 8:45, I am completely and utterly depleted. I don't get a second wind. I don't suddenly feel wired or like I can skip sleep. I just want to put on my pajamas, wash my face, and collapse into bed. 

So, no, I’ve never had even a short little burst where I felt like I didn't need rest or where I was unusually high-spirited. Even on my absolute best days, I still very much need my sleep, and my energy is just... normal, I guess? Or, well, lately, just lower than normal because of this constant heavy feeling. But never higher. I've never experienced anything like what you're describing, not even for a day or two.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a persistent depressive episode lasting at least two years, which would support a diagnosis of persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia).
doctor.question: Have you had a depressed mood most of the day, more days than not, for at least two years?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood
target_item.manifestation: Most days I can still smile for my students and get through the lessons, but underneath it feels like there’s this gray, flat feeling that follows me home and makes even my garden or watercolors seem far away.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient has experienced a depressed mood most of the day, more days than not, which directly maps to the Depressed Mood symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, yes, I suppose so. Two years... yes, it’s definitely been that long, if not longer. It's not like I'm sobbing every day, you know? I think people hear "depressed" and they picture someone who can't get out of bed, but that's just not me. I have a job to do. I have twenty-eight fourth graders depending on me, and you can't just check out when you're in a classroom. You have to be present. You have to put on a face. 

So most days, I can still smile for my students. I can get through the lessons—like I said, we're reading *Because of Winn-Dixie*, and I can still put all the right inflection into my voice when I read aloud, and I can still get excited when a student finally grasps how to do long division. I can still go through all the motions. But underneath all of that... it just feels like there’s this gray, flat feeling. It’s just always there, kind of humming in the background. 

And the hardest part is that it doesn't stay at school. It follows me home. I'll walk through the door, and my husband will ask how my day was, and I just feel... heavy. It’s like all the energy I spent smiling for the kids just drains out of me the second I put my keys on the counter. And then, even the things I normally love, like tending to my plants or getting out my watercolors—which I haven't done much of lately, to be honest—they just seem so far away. It’s like I’m looking at my own life through a foggy window. 

I’ll sit on the couch, and I know I should get up and check on my fiddle leaf fig, or maybe sketch something, but that gray feeling just settles over me. It’s not a sharp, stabbing kind of sadness. It’s just... flat. And it’s been like this for a really long time. I honestly can't remember the last time I went a whole week without feeling that heaviness pulling at me, so yes, it's definitely been more days than not for at least two years. It just feels like this is my baseline now, this constant, quiet grayness.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced any significant changes in appetite or weight over the course of their symptoms, which could support a diagnosis of persistent depressive disorder.
doctor.question: Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight over the last couple of years, like eating more or less than usual or gaining or losing weight without trying?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about changes in appetite or weight, which is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, not really. My weight has been pretty much exactly the same since... well, since before we got married, honestly. You'd think with how stressful teaching can be, or with this constant heavy feeling I’ve been having, that I might stress-eat, or maybe skip meals because I'm too drained, but I'm actually very regimented about my food. I kind of have to be, with the school bell schedule. 

Our lunch period is exactly at 11:35 every single day, and we only get thirty minutes, which includes walking the kids to the cafeteria. So I always pack my lunch the night before, usually the same kind of things—a turkey and spinach wrap, maybe some baby carrots with hummus, and an apple. I eat in the teachers' lounge with Mrs. Davis, the fifth-grade teacher next door, and I always finish my whole lunch. It's just like clockwork. My appetite there hasn't changed a bit.

And then for dinner, even when I'm feeling that grayness I was telling you about, and I just want to collapse on the couch and I don't really have the energy to cook, I still eat a normal amount. My husband is really wonderful about that. If I'm too exhausted to make the chicken stir-fry or whatever we had written on our meal-prep whiteboard for the week, he'll step in and make some pasta, or we'll just order from that little Thai place down the street. I still enjoy the food, and I eat a regular portion. 

I know some people completely lose their appetite when they feel down, or on the flip side, they sit and eat a whole sleeve of cookies, but I just... I eat my regular three meals. It's probably the only thing in my day-to-day routine right now that feels completely unaffected by everything else. I still fit into all the exact same work trousers I bought three years ago for back-to-school. So, no, my weight hasn't fluctuated at all, either up or down, and my appetite is just exactly what it's always been.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt during the current episode, which would support a diagnosis of major depressive disorder.
doctor.question: Have you felt worthless or guilty, like you don’t deserve to be happy or that you’re a burden to others, more days than not?

target_item.name: Low_Self_Esteem
target_item.manifestation: I keep thinking I should be handling everything better, and when my lesson plans take twice as long or I say no to mentoring a newer teacher, I tell myself I’m letting my family and my school down.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I feel worthless or guilty, which directly corresponds to my symptom of low self-esteem where I evaluate myself as incompetent and feel I'm letting others down.

patient.answer:
Well... I don't know if I'd use the exact word 'worthless,' that sounds a bit extreme, but guilty? Yes. Oh, absolutely, yes. It’s just... I constantly have this running dialogue in my head that I should be handling everything better than I am. Because on paper, my life is fine, you know? I have a good job, a supportive husband. But I just can't seem to keep up the way I used to, and that really eats away at me. 

Like, just to give you an idea, my lesson plans. I used to be able to sit down on a Sunday afternoon, maybe put on some light music, and knock out my entire week's plans in an hour or two. Now? It takes me twice as long, at least. I'll just sit there staring at the state standards, trying to figure out the reading blocks, and it just drags on and on. And because it takes so long, it completely eats up my weekend, which means I'm not spending any real quality time with my husband. So then I start telling myself I'm a terrible wife, that I'm letting my family down because I'm just sitting at the kitchen table stressing over fourth-grade spelling lists instead of being present with him. 

And it bleeds into my professional life, too. Just last month, our principal asked if I would be the official mentor for one of the new hires—this sweet girl who just took over a third-grade classroom and is clearly in over her head. A couple of years ago, I would have jumped at the chance. I used to love helping new teachers set up their bulletin boards and figure out their classroom management. But I just... I had to say no. I knew I didn't have it in me. And honestly, ever since I said no, every time I see her looking frazzled by the copy machine, I just feel this crushing guilt. I tell myself I’m letting my school down, I'm letting my colleagues down. It's just this heavy, nagging feeling that no matter what I do, I'm just falling short and being a disappointment to the people who rely on me.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a significant loss of interest or pleasure in activities they previously enjoyed, despite their self-reported enjoyment of hobbies like reading and gardening.
doctor.question: Have there been times when even the things you usually enjoy, like reading or gardening, felt completely uninteresting or empty, even if just for a few days in a row?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about loss of interest or pleasure (anhedonia), which is not listed in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, no, not really. I wouldn't say they feel uninteresting or empty. It's more... well, like I was saying before about my watercolors and my plants, the interest is definitely still there. I still love them. I really do. 

Like, my fiddle leaf fig—I was actually just looking at it yesterday morning before I left for school, because I noticed the top leaves were getting a little dusty, and I still get that little spark of satisfaction when I wipe them down with a damp cloth and they get all shiny and green again. I still care about it very much. And I have a whole collection of succulents on the windowsill above the kitchen sink, and I still check the soil, I still rotate them so they get even sunlight. I still *want* to do these things. 

And with the watercolors... I know I said I haven't been doing it as much lately, but it's absolutely not because I don't care or because it feels empty. If I actually make myself sit down and get my paints out, and I get my good brushes—I have these really nice sable brushes my husband got me for our anniversary a few years ago, they hold water beautifully—I still really enjoy mixing the colors. I still love seeing how the pigment spreads on the wet paper, you know, doing those wet-on-wet washes. It's just that sometimes that heavy, flat feeling I mentioned makes it hard to find the physical energy to set up the water cup and tape down the paper. But the actual interest? The enjoyment? That's definitely still there once I'm doing it. 

And reading! Oh, I still read all the time. I'm actually in a book club with some of the other teachers. We meet once a month, usually at Mrs. Davis's house—she's the fifth-grade teacher I eat lunch with—though sometimes we'll go to this little bakery downtown if nobody wants to host. But I always finish the book. Even if I'm completely exhausted from grading papers, I'll curl up in bed with my Kindle, and I still get completely pulled into the story. I still laugh at the funny parts, I still get invested in what happens to the characters. 

So, no, I don't think I've ever had a time, not even for a few days, where my hobbies felt completely uninteresting. The enjoyment hasn't gone away at all. It's just... sometimes it feels like I have to wade through that gray tiredness to get to it, if that makes sense? But the things I love are still the things I love.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced early morning awakening, a key symptom of major depressive disorder and potential specifier for severity or subtype.
doctor.question: Have you had trouble staying asleep or found yourself waking up much earlier than usual, even when you didn't have to get up for work or anything?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about sleep disturbances (insomnia, early morning awakening), which is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, no, not at all. Once my head hits the pillow, I am completely out for the night. I don't have any trouble staying asleep, and I certainly don't wake up early on my own. 

I actually have a very strict bedtime routine, which I think helps. I usually start winding down around 9:30 PM because teaching fourth graders all day just completely wires your brain, and you have to consciously transition out of that mode. So I'll wash my face, put on this lavender lotion my sister got me for Christmas—it’s supposed to be really calming, and I actually do think the scent helps signal to my brain that the day is over—and then I'll read on my Kindle for about twenty minutes or so. By 10:15, my husband turns off his bedside lamp, and I am usually fast asleep by 10:30. 

And I don't wake up in the middle of the night, ever. My husband sometimes gets up to get a glass of water or to check the thermostat, because our upstairs gets weirdly drafty in the winter and he runs hot, but I sleep right through all of it. I'm a very heavy sleeper. 

As for waking up early... definitely not. My alarm goes off at 5:45 AM every single weekday. I use one of those sunrise alarm clocks, you know the ones? They gradually get brighter starting thirty minutes before the actual sound goes off, to mimic a natural sunrise. It’s supposed to be a lot less jarring than a traditional beeping alarm, which I need because I am not naturally a morning person. But honestly, even with that light getting brighter and brighter right next to my face, I never, ever wake up before the actual birdsong noise starts playing at 5:45. 

And on weekends? Oh, if I didn't have anything planned, I could easily sleep until 8:30 or 9:00. I never find myself just popping awake at dawn for no reason. If anything, because of that heavy, drained feeling I've been talking about, I usually want to stay in bed *longer*. The bed just feels so warm and safe, and it's so hard to push the covers off and face the day. So I definitely don't have that problem where people wake up at 3 AM and just stare at the ceiling with their mind racing. I sleep completely through the night, every night, just like a log.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a loss of interest or pleasure in activities they usually enjoy for at least two weeks at any point during the current episode, which would help differentiate between persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) and major depressive disorder.
doctor.question: Looking back over the last two years, have there ever been two weeks or more when you stopped getting pleasure from things you usually enjoy, like reading or tending to your plants, even if you still did them?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about anhedonia (loss of interest or pleasure in usually enjoyed activities), which is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Two weeks? No... no, honestly, not even for two weeks. I know we were just talking about my hobbies, but even if I really think back over the whole last two years, there was never a block of time like that where I just stopped getting pleasure from them. 

Like, if I think about... well, let's take the winter before last. We had that massive snowstorm right around winter break, do you remember that? They actually had to delay the start of the spring semester by two days because the plows couldn't clear the neighborhood streets fast enough, and we were completely snowed in. And if there was ever a time when I would have just given up and stopped caring about my hobbies, it would have been then, because I was so cooped up and that heavy, dragging feeling I told you about was definitely weighing on me. But I didn't lose interest at all. I actually spent that whole week propagating my spider plants. I had all these little glass yogurt jars—the ones from that fancy French yogurt, I save them specifically for this—lined up all along the kitchen island. I was so meticulous about it, carefully snipping the little offshoots, changing the water every other day so it wouldn't get cloudy, just watching the roots grow. I got so much genuine joy out of seeing those tiny white roots shoot out into the water. I actually ended up potting them in the spring and giving them away as end-of-year gifts to my homeroom parents, which they just loved. So even during my lowest, most tired points over the last couple of years, the actual enjoyment of my plants never vanished. 

And it's the exact same with my reading. I mean, I track everything on my Goodreads account, so I know for a fact I haven't had a single month where I didn't finish at least two or three books, and I genuinely enjoyed them. Just last fall, my book club read this historical fiction novel—oh, what was it called... it was one of those ones set in World War II France, it seems like half the books we pick lately are set in World War II France, doesn't it? But anyway, I was so completely invested in the story that I actually stayed up way past my strict 9:30 wind-down time just to finish it. I think I was up until almost midnight, and I was just sobbing at the ending because it was so beautiful and tragic. You don't do that, you don't cry over fictional characters like that, if you've lost your capacity to feel pleasure in what you're reading, you know? 

So, yeah, even looking back over two years, and even looking for a two-week stretch... no. That spark for the things I love has always been there. Like I was trying to explain earlier, it's really just the physical energy to initiate the activities that fluctuates for me, because I get so bogged down with school and the lesson plans. But the actual pleasure and the love for doing them? No, that has definitely never gone away.

patient.answer:
I feel like I might be repeating myself a bit here, since we kind of just went over this, but no, definitely not. Not even for a few days. I really want to be clear about that, because I know I keep talking about that heavy, drained feeling, but it never actually touches the things I love. 

Like, even during the absolute most exhausting stretches of the school year—take parent-teacher conference week, for example. That week is just... well, it's a marathon. You're sitting in those tiny fourth-grade chairs until 8:00 PM on a Thursday trying to explain to parents why their child isn't turning in their math worksheets, and then you have to turn right around and be back in the classroom by 7:15 AM on Friday. By the time that weekend hits, I am physically just a zombie. That heavy tiredness is at its absolute peak. 

But even then, even for those two or three recovery days where I can barely drag myself off the couch, my plants and my books never, ever feel empty or uninteresting. I might just lie there on the sofa and admire how the vines on my pothos are trailing down the bookshelf instead of actively getting up to prune them. Or I might just hold my Kindle and re-read a favorite chapter of a book I already know, just because my brain is too fried to process a brand new plot. But the love for it? The actual feeling of, 'Oh, I really enjoy this'? That never goes away, not even for a day. I still get that warm, comforting feeling from my hobbies, even when I'm completely tapped out physically. So, yeah, looking back, there's never been a few days where things felt empty like that.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a major depressive episode in the past, which could indicate recurrent episodes and help differentiate between persistent depressive disorder (F34.1) and other depressive disorders.

patient.answer:
Well, see, when you say a period of two weeks where I felt down... it's tricky, because it doesn't really feel like just a two-week phase that comes and goes, if that makes sense? It’s more of a constant undercurrent. 

Like, I go to work, and most days I can absolutely still smile for my students. You have to, right? Fourth graders are so perceptive, they’ll ask you a million questions if you even look slightly off. So I put on the enthusiastic teacher face, I get through all the math and science lessons, I do the silly voices during storytime, and to anyone looking at me, I'm completely fine and engaged. But underneath all that... performance, I guess... it feels like there’s this gray, flat feeling. Just this dull, heavy grayness that sits right in my chest. 

And the hardest part is that it doesn't stay at school. When the final bell rings and I pack up my tote bag, that flat feeling just follows me right out to the parking lot and follows me all the way home. It's like a shadow I can't shake. And I know I just spent all this time explaining to you how much I love my hobbies, and that is absolutely true, I haven't lost my actual love for them! But because of that constant gray mood, there are definitely days where even my garden out back, or my watercolors—I have this little watercolor station set up by the sunroom window that I usually adore—they just seem so... far away. 

It's like I'm looking at my own life through a pane of frosted glass. I know the paints are there, I know I love painting the flowers from my garden, but that gray feeling just puts this huge distance between me and the things I want to do. So I wouldn't say I lose interest in a way where I don't care anymore, but I definitely have that down, flat feeling lingering underneath everything, pretty much all the time.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has had a depressed mood for most of the day, more days than not, for at least two years, which would support a diagnosis of persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia).
doctor.question: Have you had a depressed mood most of the day, more days than not, for at least two years?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about two years and two months, since my husband stopped working outside the home and our household routine changed.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the depressed mood has lasted for at least two years, which corresponds to the duration of the symptoms.

patient.answer:
Well, yes. Actually, I know the exact timeline because... well, it’s been going on for about two years and two months, specifically. I can pinpoint it pretty exactly because that was right around the time my husband stopped working outside the home. 

He used to have this hour-long commute into the city, so he’d be out the door by 6:30 AM every morning, and I had my mornings completely to myself before I had to leave for school. I had my coffee, I did my lesson prep in the quiet, maybe watered the pothos in the kitchen... it was just a very structured, peaceful start to my day. But then his company restructured, and he transitioned to being entirely based at home. We had to completely clear out the guest room to make him an office, which meant moving all my craft supplies and my extra planters down into the basement—which was a whole ordeal on its own, let me tell you. 

But anyway, him being home just completely changed our entire household routine. Suddenly he was always there. And, I mean, I love my husband dearly, I really do, but having that dynamic shift so abruptly... losing my quiet time in the mornings, and then coming home exhausted from a loud classroom of fourth graders to find him still in the house, usually wanting to chat because he'd been isolated on video calls all day... it just threw everything off balance. 

That happened just over two years ago, maybe two months into the fall semester, and that is exactly when that heavy, gray undercurrent I was describing really settled into my chest. So, yes, it has been most of the day, more days than not, since that specific change in our routine. I kept thinking, oh, we just need to adjust to him being home, the flat feeling will pass once we find our new rhythm and figure out how to share the space all day. But it’s been two years and two months now, and that shadow just hasn't lifted at all. It's just become my new normal.
